target_year_over_year_context.explanation:
Both disclosures report Wealth segment net income results and the key drivers (revenues, expenses, cost of credit) affecting that bottom line.

Both disclosures detail the breakdown of Wealth segment revenues for their respective years. c_2023_7_D037 cites specific revenue components (net interest income and non-interest revenue) and their drivers. c_2024_7_D042 cites the same components (net interest income and non-interest revenue) and their drivers. Although c_2023_7_D037 is a broader 'Net Income' summary ID in the proposed groups, the specific revenue breakdown topic matches c_2024_7_D042. Multi-mapping is allowed within Item 7.

Both disclosures detail Wealth segment expenses and cost of credit. c_2023_7_D037 provides the 2023 expense decrease/restructuring context and cost of credit benefit. c_2024_7_D043 provides the 2024 expense decrease/restructuring context and cost of credit benefit. This is a many-to-one relationship from the perspective of the 2023 source being reused for different 2024 granular components, which is permitted.

comparisons.peer_topic: Consumer Lending net income and revenue drivers
comparisons.peer_summary: Net income for Consumer Lending increased $334 million to $3.2 billion, driven primarily by higher revenue including a $717 million increase in net interest income and an $85 million increase in noninterest income.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and BAC reported improved profitability in their respective wealth/retail lending segments in 2024, driven by a combination of expense discipline and favorable credit outcomes. C explicitly cited 'prior repositioning and restructuring actions' as a key driver for its 2% expense decrease, while BAC noted 'higher revenue' as the primary driver for its net income increase, partially offset by higher noninterest expense. Regarding credit, C realized a '$126 million' net benefit from cost of credit due to an ACL release, whereas BAC reported a provision for credit losses that was 'relatively unchanged from the prior year' at $4.7 billion, indicating a stabilizing but higher absolute cost of credit compared to C's release.

sentences.text: Wealth expenses decreased 2% to $6.4 billion, primarily driven by benefits from prior repositioning and restructuring actions, partially offset by higher volume-related expenses and technology investments focused on risk and controls and platform enhancements.

Cost of credit was a net benefit of $126 million, compared to a net benefit of $3 million in the prior year, largely driven by a higher net ACL release due to a change in the ACL associated with the margin lending portfolio.
Net income for Consumer Lending increased $334 million to $3.2 billion primarily driven by higher revenue, partially offset by higher noninterest expense.
Noninterest income increased $85 million to $5.5 billion, primarily driven by higher card income.

comparisons.peer_topic: Private Banking and Lending Loan Portfolio and Credit Losses
comparisons.peer_summary: Gross loans related to Private banking and lending were $38 billion in December 2024 and $33 billion in December 2023, with average gross loans of $45.84 billion in 2024. The provision for credit losses was a net benefit of $232 million in 2024, driven by wholesale portfolio paydowns, compared to a net benefit of $508 million in 2023 which included reserve reductions related to the Marcus loan portfolio sale.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and GS reported net benefits (credits) from credit losses in their wealth/private banking segments in 2024. C reported a '$126 million' net benefit largely from an ACL release in the margin lending portfolio. GS reported a 'net benefit of $232 million' for 2024, attributed to 'wholesale portfolio paydowns'. This highlights a shared positive credit trend in the private wealth lending space, though C's benefit was accounting-driven (ACL release) while GS's was driven by balance sheet reduction (paydowns).

comparisons.peer_topic: Wealth Management Non-Interest Expense Trend and Drivers
comparisons.peer_summary: Wealth Management non-interest expenses increased 5% to $20,618 million in 2024 compared to the prior year. This increase was driven by higher compensation and benefits expenses, primarily due to increased formulaic payouts to representatives on higher compensable revenues, partially offset by decreases in non-compensation expenses such as professional services, legal expenses, and FDIC special assessment costs.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and MS disclose specific drivers for expense trends in their wealth management divisions, highlighting different operational priorities. C reported a 2% decrease in wealth expenses, benefiting from 'prior repositioning and restructuring actions' despite higher volume-related costs. In contrast, MS reported a 5% increase in non-interest expenses to $20,618 million, driven by 'higher Compensation and benefits expenses' linked to formulaic payouts on higher revenues, offset by lower legal and professional services costs. While C focused on structural cost savings, MS experienced volume-driven compensation growth.
